title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXIII
paragraphs:
“Your horses of the Sun,” he said,
“And first-rate whip Apollo!
Whate’er they be, I’ll eat my head,
But I will beat them hollow.”

As we have seen, Fred Vincy had a debt on his mind. Although no such intangible burden could weigh down that buoyant young gentleman for many hours together, the circumstances of this debt made it unusually persistent in his thoughts. His creditor was Mr. Bambridge, a local horse dealer whose company was much sought by Middlemarch’s young men reputedly “devoted to pleasure.” During university holidays Fred had naturally needed more amusement than he had cash to pay for. Mr. Bambridge had obligingly extended credit for hiring horses and for the accidental ruin of a fine hunter, and had also lent a little money to cover billiard losses. The total was a hundred and sixty pounds. Bambridge did not fear losing his money, sure that young Vincy had people behind him, but he wanted a document to show for it. Fred first signed a promissory note himself; three months later he renewed it with Caleb Garth’s signature as security. On both occasions he had felt certain he would pay it himself, possessing ample funds in his own optimism. You will hardly insist that his confidence needed a basis in external facts. Such confidence, as we know, is less coarse and materialistic. It is a comfortable disposition that expects Providence’s wisdom or our friends’ foolishness, the mysteries of luck or the still greater mystery of our own immense importance in the universe, to produce agreeable outcomes consistent with our good taste in clothes and general preference for the best of everything. Fred was certain his uncle would give him money, that luck would run his way, or that by successive swaps he would gradually transform a forty-pound horse into one worth a hundred at any moment. “Judgment” always counted as some unspecified quantity of ready cash. And even if things failed in ways only an unhealthy distrust could imagine, his father’s pocket remained, at that time, a last resort. His assets in optimism thus had a magnificent abundance. He had only a vague idea of what that pocket could hold. Wasn’t trade elastic? Wouldn’t one year’s surplus cover another’s shortfall? The Vincys lived easily and lavishly, without any new display, simply following family custom. The children therefore had no measure of economy. The older ones retained something of their childhood belief that their father could pay for anything if he chose. Mr. Vincy himself had expensive Middlemarch habits, spending on coursing, wine, and dinner parties. Their mother kept running accounts with shopkeepers, which brought the pleasant feeling of obtaining whatever one wanted without questions of payment. But Fred knew that fathers naturally bullied their children over expenses. Confessing a debt always brought a little storm over his extravagance, and he disliked bad weather indoors. Too dutiful to treat his father disrespectfully, he endured the thunder knowing it would pass. Meanwhile, though, it was unpleasant to see his mother cry and to have to look sulky instead of enjoying himself. Fred was so good-natured that his gloomy face under a scolding was chiefly a concession to propriety. Renewing the note with a friend’s signature was plainly easier. Why not? With such abundant securities in hope, he could have increased other people’s liabilities without limit, except that men whose names were worth anything tended to be pessimists. They were unwilling to believe that the universal order must necessarily please a pleasant young gentleman.

When we need a favor, we review our friends, appreciate their finer qualities, forgive their little offenses, and try to conclude of each in turn that he will be eager to help. Our eagerness to be helped is as communicable as any other warmth. Still, we always set some people aside as only moderately eager until the others have refused. Fred happened to cross off every friend but one because asking them would be unpleasant. He implicitly believed that whatever might be said of humanity in general, he at least had a right to escape unpleasantness. The idea of his ever occupying a thoroughly disagreeable position—wearing trousers shrunk in the wash, eating cold mutton, walking because he had no horse, or having to lower himself in any way—was absurd, incompatible with the cheerful intuitions nature had planted in him. He also winced at the thought of being looked down on for lacking money to pay small debts. Thus the friend he chose was both the poorest and the kindest: Caleb Garth.

The Garths loved Fred, and he loved them. When he and Rosamond were small and the Garths better off, the distant family connection through Mr. Featherstone’s two marriages—first to Mr. Garth’s sister, then to Mrs. Vincy’s—had produced a friendship maintained more by the children than the parents. They drank tea from toy cups and spent whole days playing together. Mary was a little tomboy, and at six Fred thought her the nicest girl in the world. He married her with a brass ring cut from an umbrella. Throughout his education he retained his affection for the Garths and the habit of treating their house as a second home, though contact between them and his parents had long since ended. Even during Caleb’s prosperity, the Vincys had treated him and his wife condescendingly. Middlemarch observed fine distinctions of rank. Established manufacturers, like dukes, could not limit their connections to equals, but they knew themselves inherently superior in a social sense defined with great precision in practice, however difficult to explain in theory. Since then Mr. Garth had failed in the building business he had unfortunately added to his work as surveyor, valuer, and agent. For a time he had carried it on entirely for his creditors’ benefit, living frugally and exerting himself to the utmost so he could eventually repay every penny. He had now succeeded. Everyone who did not think this a bad precedent gave his honorable efforts due respect. Yet nowhere in the world are fashionable visits founded on respect without suitable furniture and a complete dinner service. Mrs. Vincy had never felt comfortable with Mrs. Garth, whom she often described as a woman who had worked for her bread, meaning she had taught before marriage. Familiarity with Lindley Murray’s grammar and Mangnall’s Questions then resembled a draper’s knowledge of calico trademarks or a courier’s knowledge of foreign countries: no woman with better circumstances needed it. Since Mary had begun keeping house for Mr. Featherstone, Mrs. Vincy’s dislike of the Garths had hardened through fear that Fred might become engaged to this plain girl whose parents “lived so modestly.” Fred knew this and never mentioned his visits to Mrs. Garth at home. Lately he had visited more often, his growing love for Mary drawing him closer to everyone belonging to her.

Fred took his request to Mr. Garth’s small office in town and obtained consent without much difficulty. All Caleb’s painful experience had failed to make him careful about his own affairs or suspicious of people who had not proved untrustworthy. He thought very highly of Fred and was “certain the lad would turn out well—a frank, affectionate fellow, sound at bottom—you could trust him with anything.” That was Caleb’s psychological reasoning. He was one of those rare men strict with themselves and lenient with others. He felt a kind of shame about his neighbors’ mistakes and disliked mentioning them. He was therefore unlikely to turn his mind from the best way to harden timber and other ingenious practical matters in order to anticipate such mistakes. Before he could blame anyone, he had to move all the papers within reach, draw several diagrams with his stick, or calculate with the loose change in his pocket. He would rather do another man’s work than criticize how it was done. I fear he was poor at enforcing discipline.

Fred explained the debt, his wish to pay without troubling his father, and his certainty that the money would be ready in time to inconvenience nobody. Caleb pushed up his spectacles, listened, looked into his favorite’s clear young eyes, and believed him. He did not distinguish confidence about the future from truthfulness about the past. Still, he thought the occasion required a friendly hint about conduct and that a fairly stern warning should precede his signature. He took the paper, lowered his spectacles, examined the available space, reached for his pen and inspected it, dipped it in ink and inspected it again. Then he pushed the paper a little away, raised his spectacles once more, and let the outer ends of his bushy eyebrows droop further, giving his face its distinctive gentleness. Forgive these details for once; had you known Caleb Garth, you would have learned to love them. In a reassuring voice he said:
“Bad luck, eh, damaging the horse’s knees? And these swaps don’t pay when you’re dealing with sharp horse traders. You’ll be wiser next time, my boy.”

Then Caleb lowered his spectacles and wrote his signature with his customary care. Whatever business he undertook, he did properly. For a moment he tilted his head and studied the large, well-proportioned letters and final flourish. He handed the paper to Fred, said goodbye, and immediately returned to his absorption in plans for Sir James Chettam’s new farm buildings.
Whether his interest in the work drove the signature from his memory, or for some reason more conscious, Caleb left Mrs. Garth entirely unaware of the affair.

Since then Fred’s sky had changed, altering his view of the distance. That was why Mr. Featherstone’s gift had mattered enough to make his color come and go, first through an expectation too precisely formed and then through a matching disappointment. His failed examination had made his accumulated college debts still less forgivable to his father, and an unprecedented storm had broken at home. Mr. Vincy swore that if there was any more of the same, Fred could leave and earn his living however he could. He had never quite recovered his cheerful manner towards his son, who had especially enraged him by announcing at that point that he did not want to become a clergyman and would rather not continue in that direction. Fred knew he would have been treated more severely if the family had not shared his private belief that he was Mr. Featherstone’s heir. The old gentleman’s pride and apparent fondness served in place of exemplary conduct, just as a young nobleman’s theft of jewels is called kleptomania and discussed with a philosophical smile. Nobody thinks of sending him to a reformatory like a ragged boy who steals turnips. In fact, unspoken expectations of Uncle Featherstone’s intentions determined how most of Middlemarch viewed Fred. In his own mind, what the uncle might do in an emergency—or simply as luck embodied—always formed an immeasurable depth of airy perspective. But a gift of banknotes, once given, could be measured. Set against the debt, it left a shortfall still to be supplied by Fred’s judgment or luck in another form. The episode of the alleged borrowing, when he had used his father to obtain Bulstrode’s certificate, provided a fresh reason not to ask him for money towards the real debt. Fred was perceptive enough to foresee that anger would blur distinctions. His denial of borrowing expressly against his uncle’s will would be treated as a lie. He had told his father one troublesome matter and concealed another. In such cases full disclosure always makes the earlier account seem deceitful. Fred prided himself on avoiding lies, even little fibs. He often shrugged and grimaced at what he called Rosamond’s fibs—only brothers can connect such ideas with a beautiful girl. He would accept some trouble and self-restraint rather than be accused of falsehood. That inward pressure had driven him to the sensible act of leaving eighty pounds with his mother. It was unfortunate he had not handed it directly to Mr. Garth. But he intended to complete the sum with another sixty. To that end he had kept twenty in his pocket as seed grain which, planted with judgment and watered by luck, might yield more than three times itself. A poor rate of increase, when the field is a young gentleman’s boundless soul with every number at its command.

Fred was not a gambler in the special, diseased sense: he did not need to hang all his nervous energy upon a chance or risk as a drunkard needs spirits. He merely tended towards that more general form of gambling which has no alcoholic intensity, but circulates with the healthiest, well-nourished blood. It sustains a cheerful activity of imagination, shaping events to desire. Certain of fair weather for itself, it sees only the advantage to others of coming aboard. Optimism enjoys any throw because success seems assured, and finds a still more generous pleasure in offering as many people as possible a share in the stake. Fred liked games, especially billiards, as he liked hunting or steeplechasing. Needing money and hoping to win only increased the attraction. But his twenty pounds of seed grain had been sown fruitlessly on the seductive green field, at least whatever had not already scattered along the roadside. With payment almost due, he had nothing left except the eighty pounds kept by his mother. The broken-winded horse he rode represented a gift Uncle Featherstone had made long before. His father always allowed him to keep a horse; Mr. Vincy’s own habits made that seem a reasonable requirement even for a rather exasperating son. The horse was Fred’s property, then, and anxiety over the approaching payment made him resolve to sacrifice a possession without which life would be scarcely worth living. He felt heroic in making the resolution, driven to heroism by fear of breaking his word to Mr. Garth, by love for Mary, and by awe of her judgment. He would go to Houndsley horse fair the following morning and simply sell the horse, returning with the money by coach? Well, it would scarcely fetch thirty pounds, and who knew what might happen? Refusing luck in advance would be foolish. It was a hundred to one that some good opportunity would appear. The longer he considered it, the less possible it seemed that none would, and the less reasonable to go without the ammunition needed to secure it. He would ride with Bambridge and Horrock, the veterinary surgeon. Without asking outright, he would effectively gain the benefit of their opinions. Before leaving, he collected the eighty pounds from his mother.

Most people who saw Fred riding out with Bambridge and Horrock, obviously bound for Houndsley horse fair, assumed young Vincy was chasing pleasure as usual. Without his unusual awareness of serious business, he too would have felt he was indulging himself and doing what one expected of a lively young fellow. Fred was not coarse. He rather looked down on the speech and manners of men who had not attended university, and had written verses as pastoral and innocent of sensuality as his flute playing. His attraction to Bambridge and Horrock was therefore interesting. Love of horses alone could not explain it without the mysterious power of Naming that directs so much human choice. Under any label except “pleasure,” their company would surely have seemed monotonous. Arriving with them at Houndsley on a drizzly afternoon, dismounting at the Red Lion on a street darkened by coal dust, and dining in a room furnished with a county map glazed in dirt, a bad portrait of an unidentified horse in a stable, His Majesty George the Fourth complete with legs and cravat, and several lead spittoons might have seemed hard work. Only the sustaining force of a name made pursuing these things “gay.”

Mr. Horrock did possess an apparent unfathomable depth that gave the imagination scope. His clothes instantly suggested a thrilling connection with horses. The hat brim alone was enough: it tilted upward just sufficiently to avoid any suspicion of turning down. Nature had given him narrow eyes, with nose, mouth, and chin seeming to follow the same moderate upward slope as the brim. The result was a faint, unchanging, skeptical smile. No expression exercises greater tyranny over an impressionable mind. Accompanied by enough silence, it creates a reputation for unbeatable understanding, an inexhaustible store of humor too dry to flow and probably hardened into a motionless crust, and a critical judgment which, if you could ever obtain it, would be the one definitive opinion. This face appears in every occupation, but perhaps nowhere has it held more power over England’s young men than in an expert on horses.

When Fred asked about his horse’s fetlock, Mr. Horrock turned sideways in the saddle and watched its movement for three minutes. Then he faced ahead, twitched his reins, and remained silent, his profile no more or less skeptical than before.

This contribution to conversation was devastatingly effective. It stirred conflicting passions in Fred: a mad wish to beat an opinion out of Horrock, restrained by his eagerness to preserve the advantage of Horrock’s friendship. There was always the chance that, at the right moment, Horrock might say something priceless.

Mr. Bambridge was more forthcoming and seemed to spend his opinions freely. Loud and robust, he was sometimes described as “given to indulgence,” chiefly in swearing, drinking, and beating his wife. Some people who had lost money through him called him vicious. He regarded horse dealing as the finest of the arts and might plausibly have argued that morality had nothing to do with it. Undeniably prosperous, he bore his drinking better than others bore moderation and flourished, on the whole, like a green bay tree. His conversation had a narrow range. Like the fine old tune “Drops of Brandy,” it eventually gave the feeling of circling back on itself in a way that could make weaker heads dizzy. Yet several Middlemarch circles felt that a small dose of Bambridge lent them tone and character. He was a distinguished presence in the Green Dragon’s bar and billiard room. He knew stories about racing heroes and clever tricks played by marquesses and viscounts, apparently proving that noble blood asserted its superiority even among swindlers. But his memory’s precise tenacity was chiefly devoted to horses he had bought and sold. Years later he still passionately asserted how many miles one could trot in no time without sweating, helping his listeners imagine it by solemnly swearing they had never seen the like. In short, Mr. Bambridge was a man of pleasure and a lively companion.

Being subtle, Fred did not tell his friends he meant to sell his horse. He wanted to discover their real estimate of its value indirectly, unaware that a real opinion was the last thing likely to be extracted from such eminent judges. Mr. Bambridge had no weakness for offering praise freely. Never before had he been so struck by the unfortunate bay’s noisy breathing, a defect so extreme that only the roundest word for damnation could convey it.

“You made a bad swap when you went to anyone but me, Vincy! You never rode a finer horse than that chestnut, and you traded him for this brute. Put him into a canter and he sounds like twenty men sawing wood. I’ve heard only one worse roarer in my life, a roan belonging to Pegwell, the corn dealer. He drove it in his gig seven years ago and tried to sell it to me. I said, ‘No thanks, Peg. I don’t deal in wind instruments.’ That’s what I said. The joke went all round the county. But what the hell! That horse was a penny trumpet beside yours.”
“You just said his was worse,” said Fred, more irritable than usual.
“Then I told a lie,” Mr. Bambridge said emphatically. “There wasn’t a penny’s difference.”
Fred spurred his horse, and they trotted on for a while. When they slowed again, Mr. Bambridge added:
“Mind you, the roan was a better trotter.”
“I’m satisfied with his paces,” said Fred, needing all the support he could draw from the knowledge that this was lively company. “I’d say his trot is remarkably clean, wouldn’t you, Horrock?”
Mr. Horrock gazed ahead as neutrally as a portrait by an old master.

Fred abandoned the mistaken hope of an honest opinion. On reflection, however, he decided Bambridge’s criticism and Horrock’s silence were both encouraging: they must think better of the horse than they cared to admit.

That very evening, before the fair began, Fred believed he saw a profitable chance to dispose of his horse, one that made him congratulate himself on bringing the eighty pounds. A young farmer acquainted with Bambridge came into the Red Lion and began discussing the sale of a hunter. He called it Diamond at once, as though it were a public figure. About to marry and give up hunting, he wanted only a useful riding horse that could also pull a vehicle when required. Diamond was in a friend’s stable a little way off, and there was still time to inspect him before dark. They reached it through a back street where poisoning without the expense of drugs would have been as easy as in any grim street of that unsanitary age. Fred had no brandy to protect him from disgust, unlike his companions. But the hope that he had finally found a horse on which he could make money excited him enough to take him back first thing the next morning. He was certain that, if he did not strike a bargain with the farmer, Bambridge would. Pressure, he felt, was sharpening his intelligence and giving suspicion all its powers of invention. Bambridge had criticized Diamond in a way he never would have done to a friend’s horse unless he meant to buy it. Everyone who examined the animal, even Horrock, was plainly impressed. To benefit fully from the company of such men, one must draw inferences rather than be a simpleton taking their words literally. Diamond was dapple gray, and Fred happened to know that Lord Medlicote’s man was looking for exactly such a horse. After all his criticism, Bambridge let slip later, while the farmer was absent, that he had seen worse horses sell for eighty pounds. Certainly he contradicted himself twenty times, but when you knew what was likely to be true, you could test a man’s admissions. Fred also had to give some value to his own judgment of horses. The farmer had examined his respectable, if broken-winded, mount long enough to show interest. Probably he would take it and twenty-five pounds in exchange for Diamond. Selling the new horse for at least eighty would then leave Fred fifty-five pounds ahead and a hundred and thirty-five towards the debt. The temporary shortfall falling on Mr. Garth would be no more than twenty-five pounds. By the time Fred dressed hurriedly the next morning, he saw the importance of seizing this rare opportunity so clearly that, even if both Bambridge and Horrock had advised against it, he would not have mistaken their words for their real intentions. He would have known those deep operators held other interests besides a young man’s welfare. With horses, distrust was the only guide. But skepticism can never, as we know, be applied completely, or life would stop. We must believe in something and act. Whatever we call that something, it is effectively our own judgment, even when it looks like the most slavish reliance on someone else. Fred trusted his excellent bargain. Before the fair was properly underway, he owned the dapple gray, in exchange for his old horse and thirty pounds, only five more than he had expected.

He felt somewhat anxious and tired, perhaps from the mental debate. Without waiting for the fair’s further pleasures, he set off alone on the fourteen-mile journey home, intending to ride quietly and keep the horse fresh.
